title: The History of Cinema in the Station District
subtitle: Auf den Spuren verschwundener Kinos

textContents.body: Frankfurt was once a cinema mecca. Since the inven­tion of film, over 100 theaters have opened throughout the city—in the peak year of 1959, as many as 85 movie theaters were in ope­ra­tion at the same time. Today, very little of that remains visi­ble. Many buildings have been repur­po­sed, renovated, or demolis­hed, and names and memories have faded. With our guided tour, we invite you to join us on a jour­ney through the his­tory of cinema.

Frankfurt’s cinema his­tory actually began in a place one would hardly expect today: the sta­tion district. Between the main train sta­tion and down­town, a pres­tigious “Gründerzeit”-style neighborhood deve­l­o­ped in the late 19th cen­tury, featuring imposing facades, elegant shops, and sophis­ticated cafés. Kai­ser­strasse was considered Frankfurt’s main tho­roughfare and commer­cial street par excel­lence—a pro­me­nade for the middle class with a cosmo­po­li­tan flair. It was in this upscale set­ting that the city’s first perma­nent movie theaters began to open in 1906. Their loca­tion in the heart of this pres­tigious busi­ness district shows that, from the very begin­ning, cinema in Frankfurt aspired to be more than mere entertainment for the mas­ses.

The tour begins at Frankfurt Cen­tral Sta­tion and fol­lows Kai­ser­strasse, with brief detours into the adja­cent streets. Some his­to­ric buildings still stand, while others we must recon­struct in our minds with the help of descrip­ti­ons and pictu­res.

The tour tra­ces the his­tory of cinema from its precur­sors in the 19th cen­tury through the late 20th cen­tury. It explo­res not only pla­ces and buildings but also the evo­lu­tion of pro­gramming and audi­ences, as well as the shifting role of cinema within the urban fabric.

This tour was deve­l­o­ped during the 2024–25 win­ter semes­ter by students at Goe­the Uni­ver­sity Frankfurt. It was created as part of the semi­nar “Cinema His­tory as Urban His­tory: Topographical Per­spec­tives on an Invisi­ble Culture”, led by Andrea Hal­ler and Svetlana Svyatskaya.

We would like to thank Claudia Schüs­s­ler of the Insti­tute for the His­tory of Frankfurt for her assis­tance with image rese­arch and digitiza­t­ion.

The goal was to make the his­tory of Frankfurt’s cinema—using the Bahnhofsvier­tel as an example—visi­ble and tangi­ble once again.

We hope we have suc­ceeded.

Anke Gross, Fran Evers, Johanna Fieber­ling, Aline Fuß, Anne Haferung, René Hanauer, Hauke Henkel, Clara Itter­beck, Ogulcan Korkmaz, Rosa Krohn, Mai Nguyen, Laura Palys, Anna Rott­län­der, Sina Sche­rer, Mariia Senoko­sova, Carla Sternburg
Im Aus­schnitt aus G.I. BLUES (USA 1960, R.: Norman Tau­rog) sind bei der Fahrt durch die Bahnhof­straße drei Frankfur­ter Kinos zu sehen: das AKI, das Schu­mann-Thea­ter und das Luxor.

steps.title: Welcome to the Gallus – A District in Transition

textContents.body:
When the S-Bahn stops at Gallus­warte, you exit through Exit B onto Franken­allee and enter a neighborhood with a rich past and a changing present. Here, where brick façades meet con­struc­tion sites, our walk begins [see M0.1].

Gallus took shape in the late 19th cen­tury during indus­trializa­t­ion. Factories and compa­nies such as Adler, VDO, and Hartmann & Braun pro­vided workers’ families with hou­sing close to their work­pla­ces [see M0.2].

From the 1970s onward, many factories clo­sed, and jobs were lost. At the same time, migra­tion, affor­dable hou­sing, and gro­wing social diver­sity came to shape the neighborhood. In the 2000s, the area began to change once again: urban rene­wal, inves­tment, and large-scale new con­struc­tion pro­je­cts such as the Euro­pavier­tel pla­ced Gallus at the heart of Frankfurt’s urban deve­lopment strategies – with direct con­sequen­ces for its residents.

For the past 15 years, the district has been undergo­ing rapid trans­forma­tion. Its cen­tral loca­tion, pro­xi­mity to the trade fair grounds, and the banking district have made Gallus incre­asin­gly attrac­tive to inves­tors. Large-scale pro­je­cts – above all the Euro­pavier­tel – are drawing in new, more aff­luent residents. At the same time, long-term ten­ants are under pressure: rents are rising, moder­niza­t­ion measu­res are announced, and old ren­tal contracts are being termi­nated.

In this audio walk, we tell the story of Gallus and the stories of the people who live here. We fol­low a ten­ant named Ilse through six stops along the way [see M0.3].

title: Carl Theodor Reiffenstein
subtitle: A Frankfurt artist explores the old town

steps.title: A Frankfurt artist explores the old town

textContents.body:
Explore Frankfurt’s 19th-cen­tury Old Town with local landscape artist Carl Theodor Reiffenstein (1820-1893)!

Born in Grau­ben­gasse lane (today the Kleinmarkthalle), Reiffenstein grew up in the heart of the Old Town. Every free hour he had, he spent sketching sce­nes in his home town and surroundings. He found his main motifs not just in the Old Town’s buildings, streets and squa­res, but also in the city walls, courtyards and gar­dens.

In 2,000 water­co­lours and drawings and over 2,400 manu­script pages, he captured his impres­si­ons of 19th-cen­tury Frankfurt. Usually he drew the sce­nes on site in pencil, later turning his drawings into water­co­lour sket­ches. His extensive wri­tings describe pla­ces and details of architectu­ral his­tory, as well as recor­ding his­to­rical events and anec­do­tes.

Many pla­ces Reiffenstein documented no lon­ger exist; just a few have survived unch­anged or were recon­structed.

textContents.body:
Ein Spaziergang von Jürgen Schwab für das Kultur­amt der Stadt Frankfurt im Jahr 2025 aus Anlass des 20. Todes­tages von Albert Mangelsdorff.

Herzlich will­kommen bei diesem Spaziergang, der in 9 Sta­tio­nen vom Hauptfriedhof bis zum Dialogmuseum führt. Er ist als Audio-Walk kon­zi­piert. Sie genießen ihn am bes­ten mit Kopf­hörern. Ralph Mangelsdorff, Chris­tof Lauer, Wolfgang Haffner, Wolfgang Sandner u.a. erzäh­len von ihren Begeg­nun­gen mit dem Posau­nis­ten, der außer­dem selbst zu Wort kommt, vor allem natür­lich musikalisch! Jede Sta­tion ist übrigens nach einer Kompo­si­tion von ihm benannt. 

Die Wege zwi­schen den Sta­tio­nen kön­nen Sie mit einer Naviga­ti­ons­app zurück­le­gen. Um den jeweils ruhigs­ten, grüns­ten Weg zur nächs­ten Sta­tion zu neh­men, wie es auch unser Prot­ago­nist getan hätte, folgen Sie am bes­ten den Weg­be­schreibun­gen. Dort wird auch erklärt, wie Sie den rela­tiv lan­gen Weg vom Hes­si­schen Rundfunk zur Musikhoch­schule mit der U-Bahn abkür­zen kön­nen.
